transcript:
Header:
- Date: 2027-08-10
- Time: 10:00 UTC
- Duration: 45m
- Platform: Zoom (recording)
- Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood CSM), Priya Kumar (Northshore - Head of Platform), Tom Reynolds (SRE), Sara Lee (ML Eng), Michael O'Neil (Security)

Summary: Weekly POC check-in, focus on latency tuning (TTFT, streaming behavior, sequence length, kernel choices). Reviewed recent benchmark drop on streaming long contexts; identified next steps to run kernel sweep and test chunking strategies.

00:00 Avery Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
00:04 Priya Kumar: yep, all good. thanks a lot.
00:06 Avery: quick agenda — recaps from last week, bench numbers, marcus will walk kernel/streaming options, then we'l pick action items. sound good?
00:12 Tom Reynolds: sounds good — we've got folks on schedule.
00:18 Marcus Patel: alright, i pulled the latest bench — the weird bit is TTFT for the 1k+ token streams, we see an unexpected 80 to 120 ms bump at p50 and p95, depending on sequence distribution. i'm going to share my screen...
00:33 Sara Lee: yeah that's what we saw locally too, we thought maybe our client buffering but we double checked.
00:40 Marcus: ok, so two possibilities — kernel selection on the runtime is picking a slower aten fallback for long seqs, or the streaming chunk size is too small causing repeated kernel launches. also kv cache warmup behavior matters.
00:55 Priya: can you explain aten fallback? i heard that earlier in the doc but not sure.
01:00 Marcus: sure — so our runtime chooses optimized kernels based on sequence length and layer shapes; for some model variants at long seq lengths it falls back to more generic aten kernels which are less optimized on that GPU, so you see higher per-token latency. sometimes also memory layout forces extra memcpy.
01:20 Michael O'Neil: is that something we can control from the config or it's internal?
01:24 Marcus: we can influence it — there are runtime flags to prefer aggressive kernel-specialization or force a specific kernel path; but that can change throughput and memory utilization. it's a tradeoff.
01:32 Avery: and to add, quantization profile matters too — 4-bit vs 8-bit shaves memory but may need different kernels. sara, you mentioned client buffering, can you walk through what you're sending?
01:45 Sara: sure — our flow is user prompt ~200 tokens then model generates up to 1k, in streaming we chunk at 64 tokens right now and flush after each chunk. we thought that'd keep steady latency but it seems to cause repeated kernel invocations.
01:58 Marcus: yep chunk size 64 is quite small for long generations; that exacerbates kernel launch overhead. Try 128-256 tokens per chunk as a test. also check prefix caching — if the prefix isn't cached across requests you'll pay warmup every call.
02:12 Tom: on prefix caching, we route via our VPC peered setup, is there anything special to enable caching?
02:19 Marcus: nothing special, but if you use per-request unique user ids or ephemeral keys we won't hit the cache. also KV cache lives on the serving side; if you pin to a dedicated worker the KV stays hot. in the hosted test we saw better p95 when pinned.
02:33 Priya: pinned to dedicated workers — that implies dedicated pool which we might need for latency SLOs. pricing wise how sensitive is that?
02:40 Avery: dedicated will increase cost but gives predictable latency. we'll send price delta in the spreadsheet. we'll also show commit vs burst options.
02:48 Michael: about streaming vs non-streaming, we worry about TTFT (time to first token) more than aggregate throughput, because frontend UX is impacted.
02:56 Marcus: TTFT is often dominated by initial kernel selection + model load for cold starts. For streaming, small chunk flushes add overhead. So two levers: reduce cold path (keep warm via pinned workers or longer lease) and increase chunk size to reduce kernel launch frequency.
03:12 Sara: would increasing chunk size hurt perceived streaming interactivity? if we do 256 tokens chunking, the first token still needs to appear quickly right?
03:20 Marcus: good point — you can implement a hybrid: send a small initial chunk (say first token or first 8 tokens) eagerly and then batch subsequent tokens in larger chunks. that's what we call progressive flushing. it gets you better TTFT while reducing kernel churn.
03:32 Priya: can Redwood runtime do progressive flush natively or is that client-side?
03:36 Marcus: currently it's client-side behavior — we stream partial tokens as they arrive. but we have SDK helpers and example code for progressive flush; we'll drop a snippet in the repo.
03:45 Avery: ok next, kernel sweep plan — marcus?
03:47 Marcus: i'll run a sweep across kernel choices (specialized fp16 kernels, quantized int4 paths, aten fallback) for the 1k token profile with chunk sizes 64/128/256 and measure TTFT, p50, p95 and throughput. i'll include profiling traces showing memcpy and kernel launch counts.
04:03 Sara: can you also include sequence-length truncated tests? like 256/512/1024 to see where the cliff is.
04:08 Marcus: yep will do.
04:10 Priya: any quick wins we can try today?
04:12 Marcus: change chunking to 128, pin a dedicated worker for a short run, and enable our moderate specialization flag — that usually helps p95 by ~20-30 ms in our internal tests.
04:22 Tom: network hairpins — any impact from our VPC peering? we use transit gateway and there's NAT for egress, could that add latency?
04:28 Marcus: network adds jitter but the magnitudes we see are small (5-15 ms) compared to kernel overhead. still worth measuring end-to-end. please capture tcp pings and we can correlate.
04:36 Michael: on security/compliance, we'll need SOC2 docs and audit logs. last week you mentioned audit log retention in private deployments — can you resend that?
04:44 Avery: yes, we'll attach the SOC2 and the audit log retention doc. for private/on-prem we can provide HSM/KMS options as well.
04:52 Priya: one more question — kernel changes sound a bit risky for stability, what's Redwood's rollback story?
04:56 Marcus: kernel flags are per-deployment; we can A/B or canary a kernel change, and route a percentage of traffic. our runtime supports canary rollouts and automatic fallback if error rate spikes.
05:06 Sara: great. on the model side, we are using redwood-v2-7b-quantized in these tests — is there a recommended variant for low TTFT?
05:13 Marcus: generally fp16 specialized variants have lower TTFT but larger memory; quantized int4 paths reduce mem but occasionally force aten fallback on some ops. we'll include recommendations per test.
05:23 Avery: ok let's recap real quick.
05:25 Avery: action items — i'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and pricing delta; marcus will run kernel sweep with chunking and sequence-length configs; priya will confirm on-prem window and michael will share compliance doc list. We aim to reconvene next week.
05:40 Priya: sounds good — 8/17 follow-up for streaming deep-dive and 8/18 tentative on-prem test.
05:47 Avery: perfect. thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the links.
